new.definition: A syrup made by pressing the juice from sugarcane stalks and boiling it down, traditionally in open kettles, until it turns thick and amber. Nothing is taken out along the way, so it keeps the flavor of the whole cane juice: sweet, mild and caramel-like, much as maple syrup keeps the taste of the sap. It is lighter in color and gentler in taste than molasses, which is what is left after sugar has been crystallized out of boiled cane juice. On the Thanksgiving Day menu it glazed the bacon-wrapped pork tenderloin.
new.guest: Cane syrup is Louisiana sugarcane juice boiled down until it is thick, the way maple sap becomes maple syrup, so it tastes of the cane itself: sweet, mellow and a little like caramel. On Thanksgiving Day it glazed our bacon-wrapped pork tenderloin, a local sweetness against the smoky bacon.
new.kitchen: Cane syrup and molasses are not interchangeable on a recipe sheet: molasses is darker and has more bite. How and when the glaze went on the pork, and what else went into it, was a question for lineup.
new.compare: Molasses is the nearest neighbor: molasses is what remains once sugar is refined out of boiled cane juice, so it is darker and sharper, while cane syrup is the whole juice simply boiled down, lighter and milder. Sorghum syrup looks alike but is pressed from sorghum stalks, not sugarcane.

new.background: Sugarcane became the great crop of south Louisiana after 1795, when enslaved workers on a plantation just upriver of New Orleans, on land that is now Audubon Park, made the first granulated sugar known in the colony, and the sugar boom followed. Cane syrup is the plainer product of the same plant: the pressed juice boiled down whole rather than refined. The Steen mill in Abbeville traces its story to 1910, when an early freeze struck the family's cane crop and they saved it by grinding the stalks and cooking the juice down into syrup in open kettles. By 1930 the family had built a larger mill on the banks of Bayou Vermilion. Slow Food's Ark of Taste lists traditional Louisiana cane syrup among the heritage foods it works to keep alive.

new.definition: Cornmeal cooked slowly in water or stock into a porridge, long a staple of northern Italy. Served soft, it is spooned out loose and creamy; left to cool, it sets firm and can be sliced and grilled or fried. Traditional Italian polenta is ground from hard flint corn, which keeps more body than the softer dent corn behind Southern grits. On the Thanksgiving Day menu polenta sat under the bacon-wrapped pork tenderloin.
new.guest: Polenta is the cornmeal porridge of northern Italy, cooked slowly until smooth, a close cousin of our Southern grits. On Thanksgiving Day it sat under the bacon-wrapped pork tenderloin, a mild, corn-sweet base for the cane syrup glaze and the mustard greens.
new.kitchen: Cornmeal goes into simmering liquid in a slow stream while it is whisked, so it does not lump, then cooks with regular stirring until the grains are tender. Whether ours was served soft or set, and what enriched it, was a question for lineup.
new.compare: Grits are the nearest neighbor: both are ground dried corn, but grits are traditionally ground from softer, starchier dent corn and cook up creamier, while Italian polenta is traditionally ground from hard flint corn and holds a firmer, more toothsome body. Color is no test, as either can be yellow.

new.background: Polenta is older than corn in Italy. Romans ate grain mushes called puls and pulmentum, and before maize Italians cooked polenta from farro, millet, spelt, chestnut flour or chickpeas. Maize reached Europe from the Americas in the sixteenth century, and the Republic of Venice was among the first places in Italy to grow it not as a curiosity but as a field crop. After a famine in the 1590s maize spread quickly across the Venetian mainland, and cornmeal polenta became the everyday food of the northern Italian countryside, a poor man's dish for centuries before it found its way onto restaurant plates, where it is now served soft, or set and grilled, beside meats and stews.

new.definition: The leaves of the brown mustard plant, Brassica juncea. Raw they have a sharp, peppery bite; cooking mellows them and brings out a little sweetness. The curly-leaved kind, sold as Southern or curled mustard, is cooked across the South much as collards are, often slowly with smoked meat, and the cooking liquid is the potlikker. On the Thanksgiving Day menu they came with the bacon-wrapped pork tenderloin.
new.guest: Mustard greens are the leaves of the mustard plant, a Southern green with a peppery bite that softens as they cook. On Thanksgiving Day they came with the bacon-wrapped pork tenderloin, a little bitter and peppery against the sweet cane syrup glaze.
new.kitchen: Wash the leaves well, since they hold grit, and strip out the tough stems. How ours were cooked, and with what, was a question for lineup, and it matters before calling them vegetarian.
new.compare: Collard greens are the nearest neighbor and are cooked the same Southern way, but collards are broad, flat, sturdy leaves with a mild cabbage taste, while mustard greens are thinner, often frilled, and peppery.

new.background: Brown mustard is a plant of Asia, long grown from the Himalaya to China both as a leaf vegetable and for its seed. Where it first arose is still argued: extension botanists point to Central Asia, with later spread to India and China, while a 2021 genetic study points to West Asia. In the American South it became a staple cooking green, prepared much as collards are. In Louisiana they are among the greens of gumbo z'herbes, the green gumbo of Lent, also called gumbo maigre, which Creole cooks make with an odd number of greens, often seven, nine or eleven; the old saying holds that each green brings a new friend in the year ahead.

new.definition: French for sauce with pepper: the pan sauce of steak au poivre, built on coarsely crushed peppercorns. In the classic, the steak is pressed into cracked pepper and seared, then the pan is deglazed with Cognac or brandy over softened shallots and finished with cream, or with stock in lighter versions. Filet mignon, from the tenderloin, is the classic cut for it. On the Thanksgiving Day menu it came with the herb roasted beef tenderloin.
new.guest: Au poivre, said oh PWAHV, is French for with pepper: in the bistro classic, a pan sauce of cracked peppercorns, a splash of Cognac and cream. On Thanksgiving Day it dressed our herb roasted beef tenderloin, the same lean, tender cut the classic is made with.
new.kitchen: In the classic the peppercorns are crushed coarsely rather than ground fine, and the Cognac is cooked off in the pan before the cream goes in. Whether ours carried Cognac and cream, and how much pepper, was a question for lineup, and the spirit matters to some guests.
new.compare: Steak Diane is the nearest neighbor, another pan sauce of the classic steakhouse, but Diane leans on Worcestershire sauce, often with mustard, while au poivre leans on crushed peppercorns, Cognac and cream.

new.background: Steak au poivre is a dish of the French restaurant, and who first made it is disputed. In 1950 the chef of a Paris restaurant said he had created it in 1930; another Paris chef answered that he had made it first, in 1919 or 1920, and Larousse Gastronomique records versions said to date from 1905 in Paris and 1910 in Monte Carlo, so no single origin story holds. What every claim shares is the method: a steak, classically filet mignon, coated in crushed peppercorns, pan fried and served with a quick sauce made in the same pan, most often with Cognac and cream. Its nearest neighbor, steak Diane, is a steak sauced in the pan with Worcestershire, and at the height of its popularity it was often flamed at the table.

new.definition: The French potato purée, smoother, denser and richer than an everyday American mash. The cooked potatoes are pressed through a ricer or food mill, or in the old way through a fine drum sieve called a tamis, and butter, with milk or cream, is worked in gradually until the purée turns silky and glossy. Pressing rather than beating matters, because overworked potato turns gluey. On the Thanksgiving Day menu it came under the herb roasted beef tenderloin, and an herbed potato purée was offered as a side for the table.
new.guest: Pommes purée, said pom pyoo-RAY, is the French way with mashed potatoes: pressed through a fine sieve and worked with butter until silky and smooth rather than fluffy. On Thanksgiving Day it came under the beef tenderloin, and our herbed potato purée was there as a side for the whole table.
new.kitchen: The potatoes are cooked until fully tender, riced or sieved while hot, and enriched with butter and warm milk or cream, stirred rather than whipped. Which potatoes and how much butter the kitchen used, and how the herbed side differed from the purée under the beef, was a question for lineup.
new.compare: Mashed potatoes are the nearest neighbor: a mash is crushed with a masher and stays fluffy and a little rough, while pommes purée is pressed through a ricer or sieve and enriched until it is smooth, dense and glossy.

new.background: Potatoes came late to French tables. The Paris Faculty of Medicine declared them fit to eat in 1772, helped by the campaign of the pharmacist and agronomist Antoine Augustin Parmentier (1737 to 1813), who promoted them with dinners of potato dishes and is said to have given potato flowers to the king and queen to wear. French menus still honor him: a dish named Parmentier, such as hachis Parmentier, is made with potato. The purée's modern fame owes much to Joël Robuchon (1945 to 2018), who opened his Paris restaurant Jamin in 1981 and made a purée of potatoes, butter, milk and salt his signature dish; it went on to be served at his restaurants around the world.

deepen.background: The tenderloin is the psoas major, a long muscle along the inside of the spine that does little work, which is why it is so tender. Its familiar names are French, though the usage is tangled. Filet mignon means dainty fillet, yet in France the phrase usually names pork or veal tenderloin, and the French call the beef cut filet de boeuf; American English took filet mignon for beef steak, and dictionaries date its use in English to the early nineteenth century. The Chateaubriand, a thick cut from the beef tenderloin, is widely held to be named for the writer and statesman François René de Chateaubriand (1768 to 1848), whose chef is said to have created it early in the nineteenth century. Pork has its own tenderloin, smaller and very lean, safe at 145 °F after a three minute rest.
deepen.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: Herb Roasted Beef Tenderloin and Bacon-Wrapped Pork Tenderloin
deepen.guest: Tenderloin is the long, slender muscle along the spine that does almost no work, so it is exceptionally tender, lean and mild; the beef tenderloin is the cut that gives filet mignon. On Thanksgiving Day we served it two ways: beef tenderloin roasted with herbs under a peppercorn sauce, and pork tenderloin wrapped in bacon with a Louisiana cane syrup glaze.

deepen.background: The word is French. Purée is the past participle of the verb purer, to purify or strain, from the Latin purus, pure; in Old French it meant something made pure or refined, which fits a food pressed through a sieve until only the smooth part is left. English took the noun early in the eighteenth century, and the verb, to purée, much later. In the classic French kitchen cooked food was forced through a tamis, a fine drum sieve, and a ricer or food mill does the same work; a blender gives a smooth result faster but can turn starchy potatoes gluey. A purée may be served as it is, thinned into a soup, or stirred into a sauce to thicken it.

deepen.guest: Puréed means cooked and then blended or pressed through a fine sieve until smooth; the word is French, from a verb meaning to purify or strain. On Thanksgiving Day the potatoes under the beef tenderloin and our herbed potato side were both purées, silky rather than fluffy.

deepen.background: Brussels sprouts are a form of the wild cabbage, Brassica oleracea, bred to set small heads in a spiral up a tall stalk. They take their name from the land around Brussels, in what is now Belgium, where they may have been grown as early as the thirteenth century and were widely cultivated by the sixteenth; in French they are choux de Bruxelles, Brussels cabbages. No authoritative botanical history has been written, so the early dates stay uncertain. When they reached the United States is unclear too, but French settlers in Louisiana are known to have grown them. Their modern revival owes much to Dutch breeders, who in the 1990s found the compounds behind the old bitterness and crossed milder heirloom seed into modern varieties, so the sprout served today is sweeter than the one many guests remember.
deepen.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: the roasted Brussels sprouts of the Herb Roasted Beef Tenderloin
deepen.guest: Brussels sprouts are tiny cabbages that grow in a spiral up a tall stalk, named for the region around Brussels in Belgium. On Thanksgiving Day they came roasted with the beef tenderloin, and roasting browns their edges and turns them nutty and sweet against the rich beef and the pepper sauce.
